Note that the percentages (or proportions) that we got in each sample are slightly different from the population percentages. This is really not surprising. Since we took a sample of just 500, we cannot expect that our sample will behave exactly like the population, but if the sample is random (as it was), we expect to get results which are not that far from the population (as we did). Each sample is also different from the other. This very intuitive idea, that sample results change from sample to sample, is called

The sample results are pretty close to the population, and different from the results we got in the first sample.

In both the examples, we have numbers that describe the population, and numbers that describe the sample. In Example 1, the number 42% is the population proportion of blood type A, and 39.6% is the sample proportion (in sample 1) of blood type A. In Example 2, 69 and 2.8 are the population mean and standard deviation, and (in sample 1) 68.7 and 2.95 are the sample mean and standard deviation.

In Example 1: 42% is a parameter and 39.6% is a statistic.
In Example 2: 69 and 2.8 are parameters, and 68.7 and 2.95 are statistics.

model.question: A polling organization reports that 58% of the 1,024 adults it surveyed support a proposal, while government records show that 51% of all registered voters voted in the last election. Which number is a statistic and which is a parameter?

choices.text: 58% is a statistic; 51% is a parameter
choices.feedback: Correct! The 58% comes from a sample (a statistic); the 51% describes the entire population of registered voters (a parameter).

choices.text: 58% is a parameter; 51% is a statistic
choices.feedback: It's the reverse: the survey result comes from a sample, while the records cover the whole population.
One of each: survey $\to$ statistic, complete records $\to$ parameter.

model.question: Which symbol denotes the sample proportion?

choices.feedback: Correct! $\hat{p}$ (p-hat) is the sample proportion; p is the population proportion.
p (no hat) denotes the population proportion, a parameter.
$\bar{x}$ denotes the sample mean, not a proportion.
